posts.title: don't publish your first novel
posts.description: Just got off the phone with a friend of mine who has been shopping his short stories around and finding the editorial feedback to be... Interesting . We were talking about "the state of narrative" and how some folks seem to have a very utilitarian (not like that) -- "narratological" was the term my friend used, I think? -- functional approach to narratives. "What does the character want ?" becomes the focal point of the narrative, that somehow the actions in the novel need to justify themselves to the reader, because otherwise the reader will... Stop reading? And I finally said out loud to someone who writes more than I do the terrible truth that I have come to believe: Never publish the first novel you wrote. Especially not if its the one you've been working on for the last 10-15 years. It's not good. It doesn't matter how hard you work it over, or how much polishing you do to it, fundamentally, it is a labor of love and self-indulgence and you will never be able to be objective about

posts.title: "it gave you something to argue with"
posts.description: So I've been messing around with running an LLM on my computer because I want to understand the technology better and I do think it can provide me with some support in certain areas (like writing basic python scripts, to perform stupid tasks like extracting text and formatting from an html file of a ff.net page so I can save something that is personally important to me to an epub to keep on my kindle). And then I had to write a cover letter. Everyone talks about how we just have AI-created job listings getting AI-created responses, back and forth, computers talking to themselves forever. And I with the exception of a cover letter for a job I didn't get, I don't feel like I've ever written a successful cover letter in my life. (Also maybe I have a bad definition of "successful"... But I did get an interview!) So I copied the text of the job posting into my stupid LLM and asked it to write me a cover letter. I copied what it wrote into Word and set about making adjustments. posts.title: do i love my anxiety? Valuing my time
posts.description: Sometimes I wonder if living with anxiety means that the only time I really feel alive is when I feel like something is trying to kill me. Not in a "daredevil" kind of way - I'm actually extremely risk-averse in basically most areas of my life. But in a "if I can't feel my anxiety, how do I know I'm still breathing?" kind of way. Living with anxiety sucks. It means that at any moment you can be totally blindsided and overcome by the absolute certainty that you are going to die. (Which, I guess, we're all going to die, eventually, so. It's not... wrong?) But usually the "oh god I'm going to die" feeling is more immediate than the general understanding that all life must end, in time. But I'm thinking about this mostly in terms of deadlines and my general work-life (im)balance. I like working because it makes me feel like I have a goal, a purpose I'm working towards.
